analysis.one_liner: Bans Medicare payments to hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity firms or real estate trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in March 2026 and referred to two House committees; no hearing, vote, or further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar Medicare from paying any hospital or skilled nursing facility owned or controlled by a private equity fund, a corporation owned by such a fund, or a real estate investment trust. Facilities owned by those firms on the day the law takes effect would get a three-year grace period to find new ownership before losing Medicare payments, and firms would be jointly and severally liable for any penalties owed. The goal is to push private equity and real estate investors out of hospital and nursing home ownership.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who would otherwise be treated at a private equity-owned hospital or nursing home, patients who rely on facilities that PE ownership has stripped for profits and driven into cutbacks or closure, hospital and nursing home workers facing layoffs and wage cuts under PE ownership, and communities at risk of losing a local facility. Anyone who pays into or relies on Medicare has a stake in facilities not being run to extract value rather than deliver care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare patients, hospital and nursing home staff

how_it_helps.text: Ends Medicare payments to hospitals and skilled nursing facilities owned or controlled by private equity funds, corporations owned by them, or real estate investment trusts, removing those facilities from Medicare participation unless they change owners.
Gives facilities owned by covered firms on enactment a three-year grace period to change ownership before losing Medicare payments, rather than an immediate cutoff.
Imposes joint and several liability on the firm or its affiliate for any penalty or obligation a violating hospital or nursing home receives, making owners financially responsible for violations.
Guarantees notice, hearing, and judicial review under section 1128(f) before a facility is barred, giving owners a fair process to contest enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity firms or REITs would have to sell to new, non-PE owners or exit Medicare. Their investors would absorb losses from divestment and from joint liability for facility penalties. In places where a PE-owned hospital is the main local hospital, Medicare patients there could face disrupted access during any transition, and rural facilities might struggle to find willing non-PE buyers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds, REITs, and their investors

drawbacks.text: The bill cuts off Medicare payments entirely to any PE-owned hospital or nursing home, which could hurt the facility and its patients as much as the firm's owners: Medicare patients could not use that hospital, and staff could lose jobs, even in places where the PE-owned hospital is the area's main provider or where the facility is being run reasonably well.

The three-year grace period may be too short for facilities in areas where no non-PE buyer is available, risking closures or Medicare-access gaps in rural and underserved communities rather than improved care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy targets a real, documented problem: private equity ownership of hospitals and nursing homes is associated with reduced staffing, higher prices, and higher patient mortality, and the bill aims to remove that ownership model from Medicare entirely. The potential gains for patients are large, but the design is blunt: a full Medicare payment ban with a short three-year deadline could close facilities in communities with no non-PE buyer, hurting the very patients it is meant to protect. A tiered or gradual approach might have traded some ambition for less disruption risk, but the core idea addresses a serious harm with high stakes.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in March 2026, referred to the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, with no action since.

narrative.text: Rep. Mary Gay Scanlon introduced the bill on March 12, 2026.
The Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, the Energy and Commerce Committee.
No committee hearing, markup, or floor vote has been scheduled or taken, and no further action appears in the record after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill is pending and has seen no action since referral, no one has yet benefited or lost out. If it stays stuck in committee, private equity firms and REITs that own hospitals and nursing homes would remain better off than they would be under the bill, since the bill would force them to divest or lose Medicare revenue; patients and workers would not yet benefit, since no change has occurred. The bill's supporters still have the option of pursuing it further this Congress, though inaction to date favors the current owners over any would-be beneficiaries of reform.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, no one; current owners simply unaffected

for.name: Reps. DeLauro, Deluzio, Jayapal, Moulton, Thanedar, and Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as original cosponsors at introduction.

for.name: 12 additional Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, bringing total support to 12 House members plus the sponsor, all Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republicans have signed on, and no member has publicly opposed the bill.

industries.industry: Private equity firms and hospital/nursing home investment funds
industries.note: The bill would bar Medicare payments to any hospital or skilled nursing facility they own or control, ending their ability to profit from Medicare revenue in that sector, and making them jointly and severally liable for any facility penalties.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts with hospital or nursing home holdings
industries.note: The bill treats REIT ownership the same as PE ownership for Medicare eligibility, forcing REIT-owned facilities to divest or lose Medicare payments.

industries.industry: Hospitals and skilled nursing facilities overall
industries.note: Non-PE, non-REIT facilities are unaffected and might face less PE competition for acquisitions; PE- and REIT-owned facilities would have to sell or exit Medicare, which could reduce services or access in their communities during transition.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has been referred to two committees with no action since, and all 12 cosponsors are from the same party. Most bills referred to committee in a Congress never get a hearing or vote, and dual referral reduces the odds of consideration further. Absent a push to schedule a markup or a broader legislative vehicle, it is likely to remain pending without a vote this Congress.
